summary:
Kalmykia, an autonomous republic within Russia, stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, which presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors. President Vladimir Putin signed the law in 2023 prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year; no route to legal gender recognition remains open anywhere in the country.

Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage is prohibited and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. Public expression promoting non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the "gay propaganda" law by fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or up to 15 days' detention, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution. The expanded statute covers anything "justifying" gender transition.

Foreigners who breach these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official national government warnings state this explicitly to LGBT travellers. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Since the Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation in November 2023, Russian courts have issued 101 extremism-related convictions for participating in the group or displaying its symbols, with sentences of up to 12 years in prison. Within 48 hours of that ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

A Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility in December 2024.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement has grown in volume as well as severity. Cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

Human Rights Watch recorded 257 "gay propaganda" penalties imposed in 2023-24 against 22 in 2021-22, alongside 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols, mostly on social media. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.
localsOnly:
For residents of Kalmykia the national bans apply without local exception. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been unavailable since 2023, and documents cannot be amended to reflect a person's gender. Same-sex couples cannot marry, and no statutory protection covers discrimination on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation.

Displaying symbols associated with the designated "international LGBT movement", including on social media, is prosecuted as an administrative offence under article 20.3. Participation in the organisation or display of its symbols has also produced criminal convictions carrying sentences of up to 12 years.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v2.0, June 2025, page updated 12 August 2026) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
outOfScopeNotes:
The UK Home Office note contains no Kalmykia-specific information beyond the national framework, and the Human Rights Watch reporting of 30 June 2025 likewise carries no division-specific detail. Neither source documents enforcement activity, raids or official statements originating within Kalmykia itself.

No sourced information was found on the operation of document-issuing offices, medical facilities or police practice inside Kalmykia, nor on any regional incidents of violence against transgender residents. These gaps are unresolved rather than established as absent.
